Model 3: Sex-Stratified Models

Sections 5.9 and 5.10 implemented in ten reviewable steps

Author

Analysis Team

Published

August 3, 2026

Mission — model-3

Model 1 asked “what predicts absence among Canadian workers?” and answered it once. Model 2 asked it seventeen more times, once inside each chronic-condition subgroup. Model 3 asks it twice — once among female respondents and once among male respondents — which is what Section 5.9 requests. It is a self-contained estimation script: it reads the Ellis parquet, builds its own frames, runs its own selection, and persists its own evidence. Nothing in it is loaded from model-1 or model-2.

What it borrows from both is shape. The same ten steps, the same artifact roles — t6 is the deliverable table, t62 the full ledger, t61 the in-sample metrics, t63 and t64 the held-out ones, t7 the manifest — and the same helper functions under the same names. A reader who has read either predecessor should be able to read this one without relearning anything.

One thing genuinely differs, and it is the reason model-3 exists as a separate script rather than as a re-run of model-1 on two subsets. Section 5.9 asks not only for two models but for the difference between them: the stratification is there to “highlight potential differences in the determinants of absenteeism between men and women.” Two selected models cannot supply that difference cleanly, because a term absent from one of them may be absent because the association is absent, or because a penalty declined to select it — and the output does not distinguish the two. Artifacts t65, g5 and g51 answer the comparison question on a union model instead, and Step 8 explains why.

This report is built to be vetted, not merely read. As in model-1 and model-2, it is organised as ten steps, each closing with a review point naming exactly what a reader should agree or disagree with before the next step is allowed to stand.

The status of these estimates

Model 3 is the definitive estimation script for Sections 5.9 and 5.10. The fitted objects, coefficient ledgers, and fold-level metrics it writes to disk are the versioned evidentiary record for those sections. Downstream reports should read those artifacts and interpret them; they should not re-estimate. Step 10 lists every artifact with the call that reloads it.

Three caveats travel with every number here and cannot be removed by re-running anything:

  1. The intervals are not the intervals the proposal asked for. Bootstrap replicate weights do not exist in the 2010 or 2014 PUMF (inherited decision 10). Three interval variants are reported instead, two of which are explicit lower bounds on the understatement.
  2. Estimation and selection used the same stratum. The rate ratios in Step 8 are conditional on a procedure that consumed the whole stratum. Step 9 measures how much that flatters them.
  3. The female–male comparison in Table t65 is a screen, not a set of confirmatory tests. It carries no multiplicity control, and every row inherits the selection step that produced the union term set.

Research questions:

  1. What does Section 5.9 mean by “female” and “male” in files that carry a binary sex item and no gender item, and what follows from that for how this report may be worded?
  2. Do the two strata differ in composition before any model is fitted, and by enough to confound a later difference in what the penalty selects?
  3. What does the Section 5.4 LASSO procedure retain inside each stratum, and do the two strata retain the same things?
  4. What is the adjusted prevalence rate ratio for every retained term in every stratum, and how wide is the interval once the missing bootstrap is accounted for?
  5. Where do the female and male associations genuinely differ, as distinct from where the two selections happened to disagree?
  6. How well does each sex-stratified model predict on respondents it has not seen, and how stable is its selected variable list when a fifth of a stratum is withheld?

Definition of Terms

Stratum. The set of respondents of one sex within the model-1 complete-case frame. The two strata are disjoint and exhaustive: together they partition the Section 5.5 analytic sample, so every respondent in Table 3 appears in exactly one row-block of Table 5. This is the structural difference from model-2, whose seventeen subgroups overlapped heavily.

Sex, not gender. The PUMF carries DHH_SEX, a binary item, in both cycles. Neither cycle carries a gender-identity question. The report says sex throughout and does not use the two words interchangeably. Decision 31 records this; it is a property of the instrument, not a modelling choice.

Stratification as interaction. Fitting the model separately by sex allows every coefficient to differ between the sexes, including the dispersion parameter. A single set of sex-by-term interactions in a pooled model would allow only the chosen terms to differ. Stratification is therefore the more permissive of the two, which is why no interactions are introduced on top of it (decision 33).

Union model. A negative binomial model fitted, without penalty, on the union of the terms either stratum retained under the primary specification — then fitted separately in each stratum. It is the basis of the female–male comparison (decision 39). Its purpose is to guarantee that every term has an estimate on both sides, so that “not selected” is never read as “null.”

Ratio of rate ratios. The female rate ratio divided by the male one, for the same term in the union model. A value of 1 means the association is identical in the two strata. Its interval and \(z\)-test use \(\mathrm{se} = \sqrt{\mathrm{se}_F^2 + \mathrm{se}_M^2}\), which is valid precisely because the two strata are disjoint samples.

lambda.min / lambda.1se. The penalty minimising cross-validated deviance, and the largest penalty whose deviance remains within one standard error of that minimum. Section 5.5 designates the second as primary. Model 2 reversed that designation for small subgroups; model-3 does not adopt the reversal, and decision 35 says why.

Unstable term. A term whose standard error exceeds 2 on the log scale, meaning its rate-ratio interval spans more than four orders of magnitude. Such terms are marked rather than removed; their point estimates should not be quoted.

Standardised difference. For a design column, the female-minus-male difference in weighted means divided by the pooled standard deviation. It is used in Step 2 to describe how far the two strata differ in composition, before any model is fitted.

Held out. Computed on respondents the model was not fitted to. Section 5.10 asks for held-out error explicitly, and it is not the same quantity as the in-sample error a single fit reports.

Paths, seed, the stratification variable, the four specifications, and the decision registry 
local_root <- "./analysis/model-3/"
local_data <- paste0(local_root, "data-local/")
fits_folder <- paste0(local_data, "fits/")
prints_folder <- paste0(local_root, "prints/")
path_parquet <- "./data-private/derived/cchs-2-tables/cchs_analytic.parquet"

outcome_var <- "days_absent_total"
weight_col <- "wts_m_pooled"
cycle_var <- "cchs_cycle_f"
forced_vars <- cycle_var
lasso_seed <- 42
lasso_folds <- 5

# The stratification variable of Section 5.9. The PUMF carries DHH_SEX, a binary
# item; there is no gender-identity question in either the 2010 or the 2014
# cycle. Decision 31.
stratum_var <- "sex"

# Section 5.9 names the female model first, so it is reported first, even though
# the Ellis factor orders Male before Female.
strata_levels <- c("Female", "Male")

# Section 5.10 performance cross-validation. Named apart from `lasso_folds` for
# the same reason as in model-1 and model-2: that one tunes the penalty inside
# glmnet on a Poisson deviance, this one estimates out-of-sample prediction
# error for the negative binomial refits. Both are five-fold because Sections
# 5.4 and 5.10 both say five; they are not the same folds.
perf_folds <- 5
perf_seed <- 42

# A term whose standard error exceeds this on the log scale has an interval
# spanning more than four orders of magnitude on the rate-ratio scale. It is
# reported and marked rather than removed. Decision 40.
unstable_se <- 2

# Step 9 refits every specification on every fold twice over, for both strata,
# so the block is cached. Set TRUE to rebuild.
force_refit_cv <- FALSE
cv_cache_path <- paste0(fits_folder, "cv-performance.rds")

for (folder in c(local_data, fits_folder, prints_folder)) {
  if (!fs::dir_exists(folder)) { fs::dir_create(folder, recurse = TRUE) }
}

# The canonical candidate registry, shared with model-0, model-00, model-1 and
# model-2. See scripts/modeling/candidate-registry.R for the full contract.
# What model-3 uses from it:
#   candidate_registry        52 rows, with domain, label and exclusion reason
#   lasso_vars                48; also used to define the complete-case frame
#   vars_excluding_perceived  45; the Section 5.5 primary predictor set
#   vars_including_perceived  48; the Section 5.5 secondary predictor set
base::source("./scripts/modeling/candidate-registry.R")

# The four specifications of Section 5.4, carried in full into each stratum.
# model-2 carried only two, because a condition subgroup of a few hundred
# respondents cannot support the four-way comparison. A sex stratum is roughly
# half the Section 5.5 analytic sample, so that constraint does not apply and
# model-3 answers "the same LASSO procedure described in Section 5.4" literally.
# Decision 34.
#
# Models 1 and 3 share a single cross-validated fit within a stratum, as do
# Models 2 and 4: the predictor set defines the fit, the penalty selects a model
# from it. Two predictor sets x two strata = four cv.glmnet fits in total.
model_specs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~spec_id,  ~model_label, ~perceived_health, ~lambda_rule,  ~fit_id,   ~role,
  "model_1", "Model 1",    "excluded",        "lambda.1se",  "exclude", "Primary",
  "model_2", "Model 2",    "included",        "lambda.1se",  "include", "Secondary",
  "model_3", "Model 3",    "excluded",        "lambda.min",  "exclude", "Sensitivity",
  "model_4", "Model 4",    "included",        "lambda.min",  "include", "Sensitivity"
)

# Section 5.5 designates the 1SE rule without perceived health as primary, and
# Section 5.9 refers selection back to Section 5.4 without amending that
# designation. model-3 therefore keeps model-1's ordering, and does NOT adopt
# model-2's decision 25, which reversed it for small subgroups only.
primary_spec <- "model_1"

fit_ids <- unique(model_specs$fit_id)
candidate_sets <- list(
  exclude = vars_excluding_perceived,
  include = vars_including_perceived
)

# Decisions 1 through 19 are made in model-1 and inherited here unchanged. They
# are listed by title so that model-3 is readable on its own; the alternatives,
# rationale and reversal instructions live in model-1 Table t3 and are not
# restated, because two copies of a decision drift.
#
# Decisions 20 through 30 belong to model-2 and are specific to condition
# subgroups. model-3 does not inherit them. Where one of them describes a device
# model-3 also needs - the unstable-term flag, the within-stratum design effect,
# the two cross-validation variants - model-3 re-makes the decision on its own
# account below, so that changing model-2 cannot silently change model-3.

Helpers for stratum construction, penalised fitting, and negative binomial refitting 
# Render a data frame as styled HTML for Quarto, or plainly for console use.
# Tall tables get a fixed-height scroll box so the report stays navigable.
print_table <- function(data, caption, align = NULL, scroll_height = NULL) {
  if (is.null(scroll_height) && nrow(data) > 25) scroll_height <- "600px"
  boxed <- data %>%
    knitr::kable(
      format = "html", caption = caption, escape = FALSE,
      align = align, row.names = FALSE
    ) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(
      bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE
    )
  boxed <- if (is.null(scroll_height)) {
    kableExtra::scroll_box(boxed, width = "100%")
  } else {
    kableExtra::scroll_box(boxed, width = "100%", height = scroll_height)
  }
  cat(as.character(boxed))
  invisible(data)
}

to_yes_no <- function(x) {
  factor(ifelse(x %in% c(1, TRUE), "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes"))
}

# Strip the variable-name prefix from a design column to recover the level
# label. Vectorised, because sub() uses only the first element of `pattern`.
strip_variable_prefix <- function(column, variable) {
  purrr::map2_chr(column, variable, ~ sub(paste0("^", .y), "", .x))
}

# Does this column carry any information? A factor reduced to one level inside a
# stratum cannot be dummy-coded, and a constant numeric contributes nothing.
is_informative <- function(x) {
  if (is.factor(x)) return(nlevels(droplevels(x)) > 1L)
  length(unique(x[!is.na(x)])) > 1L
}

# Apply the model-1 recoding contract to the source columns. model-3 builds one
# frame, not two: unlike model-2 it has no age-restricted item to accommodate.
prepare_frame <- function(extra_vars = character(0)) {
  ds0 %>%
    select(all_of(unique(c(outcome_var, weight_col, cycle_var, lasso_vars, extra_vars)))) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.ordered), ~ factor(., ordered = FALSE))) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.logical), to_yes_no)) %>%
    mutate(across(any_of(c("dhhgle5", "dhhg611", "dhhgl12")), to_yes_no)) %>%
    mutate(across(where(is.character), factor))
}

# Build a design matrix and the column-to-variable map that makes selection
# results interpretable. Reference contrasts; intercept dropped. Shared verbatim
# with model-1 and model-2.
build_design <- function(model_frame, term_vars) {
  model_formula <- stats::reformulate(term_vars)
  mm <- stats::model.matrix(model_formula, data = model_frame)
  assign_index <- attr(mm, "assign")
  term_labels <- attr(stats::terms(model_formula, data = model_frame), "term.labels")
  source_variable <- c("(Intercept)", term_labels)[assign_index + 1]
  keep <- colnames(mm) != "(Intercept)"

  list(
    x = mm[, keep, drop = FALSE],
    map = tibble::tibble(
      column = colnames(mm)[keep],
      variable = source_variable[keep]
    ) %>%
      mutate(level = strip_variable_prefix(column, variable))
  )
}

# Stage 1. A weighted, L1-penalised Poisson fit with the cycle indicator exempt
# from the penalty, plus the full coefficient path for plotting. Shared verbatim
# with model-1 and model-2.
fit_lasso <- function(design, outcome, weights, seed) {
  penalty_vector <- as.numeric(!design$map$variable %in% forced_vars)

  set.seed(seed)
  path <- glmnet::glmnet(
    x = design$x, y = outcome, family = "poisson", alpha = 1,
    weights = weights, penalty.factor = penalty_vector
  )
  set.seed(seed)
  cv <- suppressWarnings(glmnet::cv.glmnet(
    x = design$x, y = outcome, family = "poisson", alpha = 1,
    nfolds = lasso_folds, weights = weights, penalty.factor = penalty_vector
  ))
  list(path = path, cv = cv, penalty = penalty_vector)
}

# Extract the coefficient vector at a named lambda, joined to the column map.
coefficients_at <- function(lasso, design, lambda_rule) {
  coefficient_matrix <- stats::coef(lasso$cv, s = lambda_rule)
  tibble::tibble(
    column = rownames(coefficient_matrix),
    estimate = as.numeric(coefficient_matrix)
  ) %>%
    filter(column != "(Intercept)") %>%
    left_join(design$map, by = "column") %>%
    mutate(retained = estimate != 0)
}

# Decision 9 (inherited): a variable is promoted to stage 2 if ANY of its
# columns survived the penalty.
retained_variables <- function(coefficient_table) {
  coefficient_table %>%
    filter(retained) %>%
    pull(variable) %>%
    unique()
}

# Stage 2. Unpenalised negative binomial on the retained variable set. Wrapped
# in tryCatch so that a failure is reported rather than fatal, exactly as in
# model-2 - both strata are large, but the fold refits of Step 9 are not.
fit_nb <- function(model_frame, term_vars, outcome) {
  usable <- term_vars[purrr::map_lgl(term_vars, ~ is_informative(model_frame[[.x]]))]
  terms_used <- if (length(usable) > 0) usable else "1"
  model_formula <- stats::reformulate(terms_used, response = outcome)
  environment(model_formula) <- environment()
  tryCatch(
    suppressWarnings(
      MASS::glm.nb(
        model_formula, data = model_frame, weights = weight_scaled,
        control = stats::glm.control(maxit = 100)
      )
    ),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
}

# Huber-White sandwich covariance for a weighted negative binomial fit, with
# theta held at its estimate. The unequal-weighting component of the design
# effect and nothing more: strata and PSUs are suppressed in the PUMF, so the
# clustering component is not recoverable. Inherited decision 15.
# Shared verbatim with model-00, model-1 and model-2. If one changes, all must
# change, or Tables 2, 3, 4 and 5 stop being comparable.
robust_vcov <- function(nb_fit) {
  design <- stats::model.matrix(nb_fit)
  mu <- stats::fitted(nb_fit)
  y <- nb_fit$y
  w <- nb_fit$prior.weights
  score <- w * (y - mu) / (1 + mu / nb_fit$theta)
  bread <- stats::vcov(nb_fit)
  meat <- crossprod(design * score)
  bread %*% meat %*% bread
}

# Kish's approximate design effect from unequal weighting alone. Its square root
# is the factor by which a design-based standard error would exceed the
# model-based one if weighting were the only departure from simple random
# sampling. A lower bound. Computed per stratum, per decision 36.
kish_design_effect <- function(w) {
  length(w) * sum(w^2) / (sum(w)^2)
}

# Wald summary on the rate-ratio scale, carrying three interval variants:
#   - Wald        model-based, understates uncertainty (inherited decision 10)
#   - robust      Huber-White sandwich, sees unequal weighting only
#   - Kish        Wald inflated by sqrt(design effect), applied uniformly
# NOT bootstrap: the replicate weights Section 5.9 assumes do not exist in the
# 2010 or 2014 PUMF. Inherited decisions 10 and 15.
tidy_nb <- function(nb_fit, column_map, deff = 1) {
  robust_se <- tryCatch(sqrt(diag(robust_vcov(nb_fit))), error = function(e) NULL)

  out <- summary(nb_fit)$coefficients %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("column") %>%
    rename(estimate = Estimate, std_error = `Std. Error`, p_value = `Pr(>|z|)`) %>%
    filter(column != "(Intercept)") %>%
    left_join(column_map, by = "column")

  out %>%
    mutate(
      se_robust = if (is.null(robust_se)) NA_real_ else unname(robust_se[column]),
      se_kish = std_error * sqrt(deff),
      p_robust = 2 * stats::pnorm(-abs(estimate / se_robust)),
      rate_ratio = exp(estimate),
      ci_low = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std_error),
      ci_high = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std_error),
      ci_low_robust = exp(estimate - 1.96 * se_robust),
      ci_high_robust = exp(estimate + 1.96 * se_robust),
      ci_low_kish = exp(estimate - 1.96 * se_kish),
      ci_high_kish = exp(estimate + 1.96 * se_kish),
      unstable = std_error > unstable_se
    )
}

# Section 5.10's C-statistic, adapted to a count outcome (inherited decision 17).
# Pairs tied on the outcome carry no information about discrimination and are
# excluded from the denominator, so the comparable share travels with the
# statistic.
harrell_c <- function(observed, predicted, weights) {
  empty <- tibble::tibble(c_statistic = NA_real_, c_se = NA_real_,
                          comparable_share = NA_real_)
  if (length(unique(observed)) < 2L || length(observed) < 3L) return(empty)
  tryCatch({
    fit <- survival::concordance(observed ~ predicted, weights = weights)
    counts <- fit$count
    comparable <- sum(counts[c("concordant", "discordant", "tied.x")])
    total <- comparable + sum(counts[c("tied.y", "tied.xy")])
    tibble::tibble(
      c_statistic = as.numeric(fit$concordance),
      c_se = sqrt(as.numeric(fit$var)),
      comparable_share = comparable / total
    )
  }, error = function(e) empty)
}

# Negative binomial log-likelihood on held-out rows, using the coefficients and
# the theta estimated on the training rows. Weighted, per inherited decision 19.
nb_loglik <- function(observed, predicted, theta, weights) {
  sum(weights * stats::dnbinom(observed, size = theta, mu = predicted, log = TRUE))
}

# Deterministic fold assignment. Every specification and CV variant scores the
# same partition of its own stratum, so differences between them are differences
# in model rather than luck of the draw.
assign_folds <- function(n, k, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  sample(rep_len(seq_len(k), n))
}

# One training/testing pass for a GIVEN term set. Both CV variants of Step 9
# call this; they differ only in where `term_vars` comes from. Shared verbatim
# with model-2, including its three guards: terms that go constant in the
# training fold are dropped, test rows carrying an unseen factor level are
# dropped and counted, and a fold whose fit fails returns `converged = FALSE`
# rather than aborting the stratum.
evaluate_fold <- function(frame, train_rows, test_rows, term_vars, outcome) {
  failed <- tibble::tibble(
    n_train = length(train_rows), n_test = length(test_rows), n_unscorable = NA_integer_,
    n_terms = NA_integer_, theta = NA_real_, converged = FALSE,
    rmse = NA_real_, mae = NA_real_, loglik = NA_real_, mcfadden_r2 = NA_real_,
    c_statistic = NA_real_, c_se = NA_real_, comparable_share = NA_real_
  )

  train <- droplevels(frame[train_rows, , drop = FALSE])
  test <- frame[test_rows, , drop = FALSE]

  term_vars <- term_vars[purrr::map_lgl(term_vars, ~ is_informative(train[[.x]]))]

  factor_terms <- term_vars[purrr::map_lgl(term_vars, ~ is.factor(train[[.x]]))]
  scorable <- rep(TRUE, nrow(test))
  for (this_var in factor_terms) {
    scorable <- scorable & as.character(test[[this_var]]) %in% levels(train[[this_var]])
  }
  n_dropped <- sum(!scorable)
  test <- test[scorable, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(test) < 3L) return(failed)
  for (this_var in factor_terms) {
    test[[this_var]] <- factor(as.character(test[[this_var]]),
                               levels = levels(train[[this_var]]))
  }

  fit <- fit_nb(train, term_vars, outcome)
  fit_null <- fit_nb(train, character(0), outcome)
  if (is.null(fit) || is.null(fit_null)) return(failed)

  predicted <- tryCatch(stats::predict(fit, newdata = test, type = "response"),
                        error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(predicted) || anyNA(predicted)) return(failed)
  predicted_null <- stats::predict(fit_null, newdata = test, type = "response")
  observed <- test[[outcome]]
  w <- test$weight_scaled

  loglik_test <- nb_loglik(observed, predicted, fit$theta, w)
  loglik_test_null <- nb_loglik(observed, predicted_null, fit_null$theta, w)

  dplyr::bind_cols(
    tibble::tibble(
      n_train = nrow(train),
      n_test = nrow(test),
      n_unscorable = n_dropped,
      n_terms = length(stats::coef(fit)) - 1L,
      theta = fit$theta,
      converged = isTRUE(fit$converged),
      rmse = sqrt(stats::weighted.mean((observed - predicted)^2, w)),
      mae = stats::weighted.mean(abs(observed - predicted), w),
      loglik = loglik_test,
      mcfadden_r2 = 1 - loglik_test / loglik_test_null
    ),
    harrell_c(observed, predicted, w)
  )
}

# Cut one sex stratum out of the analytic frame and re-scale its weights to
# mean 1 (decision 37). Unused factor levels are dropped here, once, so that
# every downstream step sees the same stratum.
build_stratum <- function(frame, level) {
  frame %>%
    filter(.data[[stratum_var]] == level) %>%
    droplevels() %>%
    mutate(weight_scaled = .data[[weight_col]] / mean(.data[[weight_col]]))
}

# The candidate set offered to the penalty inside one stratum (decision 33):
# the requested Section 5.4 predictor set, minus the stratification variable,
# minus anything that has gone constant.
stratum_candidates <- function(stratum, candidates) {
  offered <- setdiff(candidates, stratum_var)
  offered[purrr::map_lgl(offered, ~ is_informative(stratum[[.x]]))]
}

# The whole stage-one pipeline for one stratum and one predictor set, from
# frame to cross-validated penalised fit. Returns everything the later steps
# need, including what it had to drop, so Table t2 can report the cost of the
# stratum restriction.
fit_stratum_spec <- function(level, this_fit_id) {
  stratum <- strata[[level]]
  candidates <- candidate_sets[[this_fit_id]]

  offered <- stratum_candidates(stratum, candidates)
  dropped <- setdiff(setdiff(candidates, stratum_var), offered)
  forced_here <- forced_vars[purrr::map_lgl(forced_vars, ~ is_informative(stratum[[.x]]))]

  design <- build_design(stratum, c(forced_here, offered))
  lasso <- tryCatch(
    fit_lasso(design, stratum[[outcome_var]], stratum$weight_scaled, lasso_seed),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )

  list(
    stratum = level,
    fit_id = this_fit_id,
    offered = offered,
    dropped = dropped,
    forced = forced_here,
    design = design,
    lasso = lasso
  )
}

Distributions

The outcome is shown inside the strata, with the pooled sample beside it, because the Section 5.9 models are fitted to the strata and the reader needs to see whether stratifying changes the shape of the outcome or only its level.

Equidispersion would put variance / mean at 1. Neither stratum is close, so
stage two is negative binomial in both, exactly as in model-1 and model-2.
The pooled row is there for one purpose: to show that stratifying does not
change the shape of the outcome, only its level. Whatever differs between
the two models will be a difference in association, not in likelihood.
Reading the stratum outcome summary

Two features govern everything downstream. The variance-to-mean ratio stays far above 1 in both strata, so stage two is negative binomial throughout, exactly as in model-1 and model-2 — and the ratio is of similar magnitude in the two, so the same likelihood is appropriate on both sides of the comparison. And the share of respondents at zero days stays high in both, which is why the C-statistic in Step 9 is a narrow instrument here and why its comparable-pairs share is reported beside every value.

Analysis

Step 1 — The Stratification Variable

Section 5.9 says “female respondents” and “male respondents.” Establishing what those words denote in terms of items that exist in the 2010 and 2014 Public Use Microdata Files is the first substantive act of the report. Unlike model-2’s condition roster, nothing is lost in the mapping — but the vocabulary is not interchangeable and the report has to commit to one.

Table t1: The stratification variable. What Section 5.9 asks to stratify on, and what the 2010 and 2014 Public Use Microdata Files actually carry. Unlike model-2’s condition roster, nothing is lost in the mapping - two requested models resolve to two fitted models - but the vocabulary matters and decision 31 records it.
Section 5.9 asks for PUMF item Carried Note
Female respondents DHH_SEX = 2 yes Coded to sex == ‘Female’ in Ellis. Reported first, as Section 5.9 names it first.
Male respondents DHH_SEX = 1 yes Coded to sex == ‘Male’ in Ellis. The Ellis factor orders Male first; the reporting order here is Section 5.9’s.
Gender identity — no Neither the 2010-2011 nor the 2013-2014 PUMF carries a gender item. This report says sex throughout and does not use the two words interchangeably.
A third or unstated category — no DHH_SEX is binary and has no ‘not stated’ code in the analytic frame. No respondent is lost to the stratification.
Sex as a predictor DHH_SEX removed Constant inside its own stratum, so it carries no information there and is removed from the candidate set (decision 33). Its pooled main effect is a model-1 quantity and lives in Table 3.

Two rows of Table t1 are the ones to read. There is no gender item in either cycle, so the report says sex and means the DHH_SEX question; and sex leaves the candidate set when it becomes the stratification, because a variable that is constant inside a stratum carries no information there.

Table t11: Sex stratum inventory. Both sample sizes Section 5.9 asks for - unweighted n and weighted N - plus the count that actually limits a count model, the number of respondents reporting at least one day absent. The design effect is computed within each stratum (decision 36). ‘Weighted days lost’ is the population total the two models are ultimately about.

Female 24,273 6,371,630 49.6% 8,608 35.5% 1.532 9,758,436 3.742
Male 24,659 7,724,915 50.4% 6,395 25.9% 1.075 8,305,939 3.518

Table t11 carries both sample sizes Section 5.9 asks for — unweighted \(n\) and weighted \(N\) — and one it does not: the number of respondents in each stratum reporting at least one day absent. That third column is the one that limits a count model, and it does not divide between the strata in the same proportion the sample size does.

Review point 1

Agree or disagree with the stratification in Table t1. Three specific questions:

  1. Is DHH_SEX the intended stratifier, or was a gender construct meant — in which case the analysis cannot be delivered from these files and needs a different data source.
  2. Should the report be worded in terms of sex throughout, as decision 31 commits it to, or is “men and women” acceptable shorthand in the manuscript despite the instrument being a sex item?
  3. Section 5.9 asks for two models. Should a third, pooled model with sex-by-term interactions be reported beside them, or does the stratification supersede it? Decision 33 records the argument that stratification is the more permissive of the two.

Step 2 — Stratum Feasibility and Composition

Neither stratum is small, so the feasibility question that dominated model-2 is not in doubt here. The question that replaces it is composition: the female and male strata are different populations, and a difference in what the penalty selects may be a difference in who is in the stratum rather than in how absence is produced.

Compute per-stratum candidate counts, design width, and between-stratum standardised differences 
feasibility <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  stratum = strata_levels,
  fit_id = fit_ids
) %>%
  purrr::pmap_dfr(function(stratum, fit_id) {
    sub <- strata[[stratum]]
    candidates <- candidate_sets[[fit_id]]
    offered <- stratum_candidates(sub, candidates)
    dropped <- setdiff(setdiff(candidates, stratum_var), offered)
    forced_here <- forced_vars[purrr::map_lgl(forced_vars, ~ is_informative(sub[[.x]]))]
    n_columns <- ncol(build_design(sub, c(forced_here, offered))$x)
    tibble::tibble(
      stratum = stratum,
      fit_id = fit_id,
      predictor_set = ifelse(fit_id == "include",
                             "including perceived health",
                             "excluding perceived health"),
      n = nrow(sub),
      n_nonzero = sum(sub[[outcome_var]] > 0),
      n_offered = length(offered),
      n_dropped = length(dropped),
      dropped_vars = paste(variable_labels[dropped], collapse = "; "),
      n_columns = n_columns
    )
  }) %>%
  mutate(
    per_column = n / pmax(n_columns, 1L),
    nonzero_per_column = n_nonzero / pmax(n_columns, 1L)
  )

readr::write_csv(feasibility, paste0(local_data, "stratum-feasibility.csv"))

# Standardised differences between the two strata, over every design column the
# Section 5.4 candidate set would produce. A dummy column's standardised
# difference is a difference in prevalence scaled by its own spread, so the same
# statistic covers factors and numerics without special-casing either.
composition_design <- build_design(ds1, setdiff(vars_including_perceived, stratum_var))

composition_balance <- local({
  x <- composition_design$x
  is_female <- ds1[[stratum_var]] == "Female"
  wf <- ds1[[weight_col]][is_female]
  wm <- ds1[[weight_col]][!is_female]
  wf <- wf / mean(wf)
  wm <- wm / mean(wm)

  weighted_moments <- function(mat, w) {
    m <- as.numeric(crossprod(mat, w) / sum(w))
    centred <- sweep(mat, 2, m, "-")
    v <- as.numeric(crossprod(centred^2, w) / sum(w))
    list(mean = m, var = v)
  }

  f <- weighted_moments(x[is_female, , drop = FALSE], wf)
  m <- weighted_moments(x[!is_female, , drop = FALSE], wm)
  pooled_sd <- sqrt((f$var + m$var) / 2)

  composition_design$map %>%
    mutate(
      mean_female = f$mean,
      mean_male = m$mean,
      difference = f$mean - m$mean,
      smd = ifelse(pooled_sd > 0, difference / pooled_sd, NA_real_),
      domain = variable_domains[variable],
      variable_label = variable_labels[variable],
      term = paste0(variable_label, ifelse(level == "", "", paste0(": ", level)))
    )
})

readr::write_csv(composition_balance, paste0(local_data, "composition-balance.csv"))

Graph g1 is the diagnostic that model-2 did not need. Every point is a design column that the Section 5.4 candidate set would produce, and its position is how far the two strata differ on it. The dotted lines mark \(\pm 0.1\), the conventional threshold below which an imbalance is treated as negligible. Columns that sit far from zero are the ones to hold in mind for the rest of the report: if such a variable is later retained in one stratum and not the other, prevalence is a live explanation and association is not the only one.

Table t2: Stratum feasibility ledger, one row per stratum per predictor set. ‘Dropped as constant’ counts candidate variables that lose all but one level inside the stratum and so cannot be dummy-coded (decision 33); the stratifying variable is removed separately and is not counted here. Both strata carry hundreds of respondents per design column, which is why model-2’s small-subgroup machinery - the n < 500 flag, the minimum-fit threshold, the reversed penalty designation - is absent from model-3.

Review point 2

Agree or disagree with three choices about the candidate set.

  1. Decision 33 removes sex and nothing else. Should any other variable be removed a priori inside a stratum — for example, items whose meaning differs by sex — or is dropping only what becomes constant the right rule?
  2. Should the standardised differences in Graph g1 carry a formal threshold that triggers an action, or are they a reading aid only? They currently trigger nothing; they exist so that a later asymmetry in selection can be checked against composition.
  3. Decision 32 filters the model-1 frame rather than re-deriving complete cases inside each stratum. Filtering keeps Table 5 describing the same respondents as Table 3, at the cost of importing model-1’s missingness rule. Is that the right trade?

Step 3 — The Stratum Samples

Output out2: Sample construction arithmetic
Source rows (Ellis analytic table):      63,843

The analytic frame is the model-1 sample, unchanged (decision 32). The two
strata partition it: every respondent appears in exactly one, and the sum
of the two is the whole. This is the structural difference from model-2,
whose seventeen subgroups overlapped heavily and summed to far more than
the frame. Nothing here needs a comorbidity correction.
What replaces it is imbalance. Design columns exceeding the conventional
negligible-difference threshold of 0.1 in absolute standardised difference:

The two strata sum exactly to the analytic frame. That arithmetic is worth stating because it is what model-2 could not state: seventeen condition subgroups overlapped heavily and summed to far more than their frame, which required a comorbidity correction before any coefficient could be read. Nothing of the kind is needed here. What replaces it is the imbalance counted at the foot of out2.

Table t21 is the specific form the composition problem takes in this study. The exposures the proposal is about — the chronic conditions — are themselves unequally distributed between the sexes. A condition retained in the female model and not the male one may be more prevalent among women, more strongly associated with absence among women, or simply better powered there. Table t21 settles the first of those three. The second is what Step 8 exists to answer; the third is what Step 9 measures.

Review point 3

Agree or disagree that prevalence differences are reported and left standing rather than adjusted for. The alternative would be to reweight one stratum to the other’s composition, which would make the two models describe a common hypothetical population but would no longer describe either observed one. Section 5.9 asks for models of female and male respondents, which is what is estimated; the reweighted alternative is a different question and is not attempted here.

Step 4 — The Decision Registry

Model 3 inherits nineteen decisions from model-1 and makes ten of its own. It does not inherit model-2’s decisions 20 through 30, which are specific to condition subgroups; where model-3 needs the same device — the unstable-term flag, the within-stratum design effect, the two cross-validation variants — it re-makes the decision on its own account, so that changing model-2 cannot silently change model-3.

Table t3: Decision registry for model-3, decisions 31 through 40. Numbering continues from model-2 so that a decision id is unambiguous across the project.
# Decision Alternatives considered Chosen Rationale Reverse by editing
31 The stratification variable sex as recorded in DHH_SEX; a gender variable; sex crossed with age or cycle sex (DHH_SEX), two levels Section 5.9 says ‘female respondents’ and ‘male respondents’. The PUMF carries DHH_SEX, a binary item, in both cycles, and neither cycle carries a gender-identity question. The report therefore says sex and not gender throughout, and the two-level structure is a property of the instrument rather than a modelling choice. No respondent is excluded by the stratification: DHH_SEX has no missing values in the analytic frame. stratum_var and strata_levels in declare-globals
32 Stratum base sample Re-derive complete cases inside each stratum; filter the model-1 complete-case frame Filter the model-1 frame Re-deriving would give each stratum its own denominator and its own candidate set, so the female and male models would not be comparable with each other and neither would be comparable with Table 3. Filtering makes each stratum a strict subset of the Section 5.5 analytic sample, and makes the two strata a partition of it. ds1 in tweak-data-0
33 Candidate set inside a stratum Keep sex in the candidate set; remove it; remove it and add its interactions Remove sex; keep everything else that is informative Sex is constant inside its own stratum by construction and carries no information there. Nothing else is removed a priori: a variable is dropped only if it loses all but one level inside the stratum, and every such drop is recorded in Table t2. Interactions are not introduced, because stratification IS the interaction Section 5.9 asks for - fitting the model separately by sex allows every coefficient to differ, which a single sex-by-term interaction set would only do for the terms chosen to carry it. stratum_candidates() in declare-functions
34 How many Section 5.4 specifications are carried One (the Section 5.5 primary); two (one predictor set at both penalties, as model-2 does); all four All four Section 5.9 refers selection back to Section 5.4, which describes four specifications on two axes. model-2 carried only the primary predictor set because a condition subgroup of a few hundred respondents cannot support a four-way comparison. A sex stratum is roughly half the Section 5.5 sample, so that constraint does not apply, and carrying all four makes Table 5 comparable with Table 3 specification by specification. Models 1 and 3 share one cross-validated fit and Models 2 and 4 share another, so four specifications cost two fits per stratum, not four. model_specs and candidate_sets in declare-globals
35 Penalty rule designated primary lambda.1se as Section 5.5 designates; lambda.min as model-2 designates for small subgroups lambda.1se, without perceived health (Model 1) model-2 reversed this ordering with decision 25, but the argument there was scale: a parsimonious penalty applied to a subgroup of a few hundred respondents frequently returns nothing at all. In model-1 the 1SE rule retained 10 variables at n = 48,932, and a sex stratum is about half of that, so the rule has something to say. Section 5.5’s designation therefore stands unamended. Table t5 reports what each rule retained in each stratum so the choice remains checkable. primary_spec in declare-globals
36 Design effect basis Reuse model-1’s full-sample Kish design effect; compute one within each stratum Within each stratum A design effect describes the weight distribution of the sample whose intervals it widens. Weights inside a sex stratum are not distributed as they are in the pooled sample, and Output out5 shows the realised value differing between the two. This repeats model-2’s decision 29 rather than inheriting it, so that the two reports can diverge without either breaking silently. build_stratum() in declare-functions
37 Weight rescaling Carry model-1’s weight into the stratum unchanged; rescale to mean 1 within each stratum Rescale within each stratum glm.nb treats prior weights as frequencies when estimating dispersion, so a stratum whose carried-forward weights average far from 1 would return a theta on a different scale from the other. Rescaling inside the stratum makes theta comparable between the female and male models. Point estimates are unaffected; only the scale of the weights changes. build_stratum() in declare-functions
38 Section 5.10 resampling method 5-fold cross-validation; leave-one-out; a single train / test split 5-fold, in both variants of inherited decision 16 Section 5.10 names five folds and, unlike Section 5.8, does not offer leave-one-out - which is consistent, because both strata are large. The term set is scored twice over: once held fixed at what the whole stratum selected (Table t63, the literal reading), and once with the entire two-stage procedure re-run inside each training fold (Table t64, the honest estimate). Folds that fail to converge are counted, not silently dropped. perf_folds in declare-globals
39 Basis for the female-male comparison Compare the two selected models term by term; compare only terms selected in both; refit both strata on the union of the two selected sets Refit on the union set Section 5.9 asks the stratified models to ‘highlight potential differences in the determinants of absenteeism between men and women’. Comparing the two SELECTED models cannot do that cleanly: a term missing from the male model may be absent because the association is absent, or because a penalty declined to select it, and the two are not distinguishable from the output. Refitting both strata, without penalty, on the union of the terms either stratum retained under the primary specification gives every term an estimate on both sides. Selection asymmetry is then reported separately, as a fact about the procedure, in the ‘Retained in’ column of Table t65. union_terms and nb_union in the t65 block
40 Rare levels and unstable terms Collapse rare levels; drop variables that have a rare level; retain and flag Retain and flag at SE > 2 on the log scale The same device model-2 adopted with decision 27, re-made here rather than inherited. It matters much less at stratum scale than at subgroup scale - both strata carry more than twenty thousand respondents - but a factor level that is rare in the population is rare in both strata, and a flagged term is cheaper than a silently uninformative interval. unstable_se in declare-globals

Inherited decision 10 records that bootstrap variance estimation is impossible with these data. Section 5.9 asks for 500 bootstrap replicate weights in the same words Sections 5.3, 5.5 and 5.7 use, and the answer is the same: CCHS bootstrap replicate weights begin with the 2015 cycle, neither the 2010 nor the 2014 PUMF carries them, and strata and PSU identifiers are suppressed.

Model 3 responds as its predecessors do — a Wald interval beside a Huber–White sandwich interval and a Kish-inflated interval — with the design effect computed within each stratum (decision 36), because the weight distribution inside a sex stratum is not the weight distribution of the pooled sample. Output out5 shows how far the two differ.

Review point 4

Read decisions 31 through 40. Three are consequential and the rest are bookkeeping:

  1. Decision 34 carries all four Section 5.4 specifications rather than the two model-2 could afford. This is what makes Table 5 readable row-for-row against Table 3.
  2. Decision 35 keeps lambda.1se primary, declining model-2’s reversal. The argument is scale, and Table t5 supplies the evidence for or against it.
  3. Decision 39 builds the female–male comparison on a union model rather than on the two selected models. This is the report’s central methodological choice and Step 8 is where its consequences appear.

Step 5 — The Four Specifications

Section 5.9 says selection should follow the Section 5.4 procedure. Section 5.4 describes four specifications, arranged on two axes: a perceived-health toggle and a penalty rule. Model 2 carried only two of them, because a condition subgroup of a few hundred respondents cannot support a four-way comparison. A sex stratum is roughly half the Section 5.5 analytic sample, so that constraint does not apply and model-3 answers the reference literally.

Table t4: The four Section 5.4 specifications, carried in full into each stratum (decision 34). The predictor set defines the cross-validated fit; the penalty selects a model from it, so two fits per stratum yield four models. Model 1 is primary, following Section 5.5 and unlike model-2, which reversed the designation for small subgroups only (decision 35). Every row has a direct counterpart in model-1’s Table 3, which is what makes Table 5 readable against Table 3.
Specification Role Penalty Perceived health Candidates offered Shares a fit with Section 5.5 counterpart
Model 1 Primary lambda.1se excluded 44 (sex removed) Models 1 and 3 Table 3 Model 1
Model 2 Secondary lambda.1se included 47 (sex removed) Models 2 and 4 Table 3 Model 2
Model 3 Sensitivity lambda.min excluded 44 (sex removed) Models 1 and 3 Table 3 Model 3
Model 4 Sensitivity lambda.min included 47 (sex removed) Models 2 and 4 Table 3 Model 4

The arithmetic in the “shares a fit with” column matters for reading the rest of the report. The predictor set defines the cross-validated fit; the penalty rule selects a model from it. Two predictor sets in two strata therefore cost four penalised fits, not eight, and Models 1 and 3 differ only in where on the same path they are read.

Review point 5

Agree or disagree that all four specifications should be carried into the deliverable table. The alternative is to report only Model 1 and relegate the rest to an appendix, which would make Table 5 far shorter and would match the way Section 5.9 is worded — it asks for “a model,” singular, per sex. The argument for carrying four is that it makes the sex-stratified table comparable with Table 3 specification by specification, and that the cost is a wider table rather than more computation.

Step 6 — Stage One, Per-Stratum Penalised Poisson

Four weighted L1-penalised Poisson fits: two strata by two predictor sets, each with its own five-fold cross-validated penalty path.

Fit and persist one cross-validated penalised Poisson model per stratum and predictor set 
fit_keys <- tidyr::expand_grid(stratum = strata_levels, fit_id = fit_ids) %>%
  mutate(key = paste0(stratum, "__", fit_id))

stratum_fits <- purrr::set_names(
  purrr::map2(fit_keys$stratum, fit_keys$fit_id, fit_stratum_spec),
  fit_keys$key
)

for (this_key in names(stratum_fits)) {
  sf <- stratum_fits[[this_key]]
  if (!is.null(sf$lasso)) {
    saveRDS(sf$lasso$cv, paste0(fits_folder, "cv_", this_key, ".rds"))
    saveRDS(sf$design$map, paste0(fits_folder, "map_", this_key, ".rds"))
  }
}

fitted_ok <- names(stratum_fits)[purrr::map_lgl(stratum_fits, ~ !is.null(.x$lasso))]
stopifnot(length(fitted_ok) == nrow(fit_keys))

fit_panel_label <- function(key) {
  parts <- strsplit(key, "__", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  paste0(parts[1], " - perceived health ",
         ifelse(parts[2] == "include", "included", "excluded"))
}
panel_levels <- purrr::map_chr(fit_keys$key, fit_panel_label)

cv_curve_data <- purrr::map_dfr(fitted_ok, function(this_key) {
  cv <- stratum_fits[[this_key]]$lasso$cv
  tibble::tibble(
    key = this_key,
    lambda = cv$lambda,
    cv_mean = cv$cvm,
    cv_low = cv$cvlo,
    cv_high = cv$cvup,
    n_nonzero = cv$nzero
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(panel = factor(purrr::map_chr(key, fit_panel_label), levels = panel_levels))

lambda_marks <- purrr::map_dfr(fitted_ok, function(this_key) {
  cv <- stratum_fits[[this_key]]$lasso$cv
  tibble::tibble(
    key = this_key,
    lambda_rule = c("lambda.1se", "lambda.min"),
    lambda = c(cv$lambda.1se, cv$lambda.min)
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(panel = factor(purrr::map_chr(key, fit_panel_label), levels = panel_levels))

path_data <- purrr::map_dfr(fitted_ok, function(this_key) {
  sf <- stratum_fits[[this_key]]
  as.matrix(sf$lasso$path$beta) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("column") %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-column, names_to = "step", values_to = "estimate") %>%
    mutate(
      lambda = sf$lasso$path$lambda[as.integer(sub("^s", "", step)) + 1],
      key = this_key
    ) %>%
    left_join(sf$design$map, by = "column")
}) %>%
  mutate(
    domain = variable_domains[variable],
    panel = factor(purrr::map_chr(key, fit_panel_label), levels = panel_levels)
  )

The quantity to read in Graph g2 is the distance between the two dashed lines relative to the depth of the minimum. That distance is how much room the penalty has: where the curve is flat over a wide range, cross-validation cannot distinguish penalties there, and the two rules will disagree a great deal about how many variables to keep. Comparing the female and male panels of the same predictor set is the first indication of whether the two strata are equally decisive.

Reading each panel right to left, the order in which coefficients leave zero is the order in which that stratum insists on them. Comparing the female and male panels of the same predictor set is the first visual answer to Section 5.9 — but only the first, and a weak one: the paths show what the penalty did, not what the associations are, and Step 8 is where the two are separated.

Review point 6

Agree or disagree with the fitting choices, which are inherited unchanged from model-1: five folds, seed 42, survey weights passed to cv.glmnet, cycle exempt from the penalty. One consideration is new. Each stratum’s folds are cut inside that stratum, so the female and male cross-validations are independent and use different respondents. An alternative would cut folds once in the pooled frame and inherit them, which would make the two penalty paths share a fold structure. Neither is obviously right; the current choice keeps each stratum a self-contained analysis.

Survey design CCHS cycle 1, 2, 3, 4 1, 2, 3, 4 both

Graph g4 is the visual form of the selection result, and it is read across the two columns of a panel rather than down. A row coloured in both columns is a predictor both sexes insist on. A row coloured in one is where Section 5.9 has something to say — potentially. The word is doing real work: an asymmetry in this grid is a fact about the procedure, and it becomes a fact about the data only if the other stratum’s estimate for that term is also small, which the grid cannot show. Table t65 is where that check happens, and Step 8 explains why it needs a different model to do it.

Review point 7

Two questions to settle before the estimates in Step 8 may be read.

  1. Should “retained” continue to mean “at least one design column survived”? Inherited decision 9 records the alternative. It matters here because a factor retained in one stratum on the strength of a single level will appear in Graph g4 as a whole-variable asymmetry.
  2. Is the asymmetry in Graph g4 worth reporting in its own right, or only as a route to Table t65? Model 2 reported its selection grid as a central artifact because cross-condition recurrence was itself a finding. Here the analogous claim would be weaker, since two columns cannot establish a pattern the way seventeen can.

Step 8 — Stage Two, Negative Binomial Estimation

Each retained set is re-estimated without penalty under a negative binomial likelihood, inside its own stratum. This step answers Section 5.9 and produces deliverable Table 5. Before the estimates, the instruments used to bracket their uncertainty.

Fit and persist the eight sex-stratified negative binomial models 
nb_keys <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  stratum = strata_levels,
  spec_id = model_specs$spec_id
) %>%
  mutate(key = paste0(stratum, "__", spec_id))

spec_terms <- purrr::set_names(
  purrr::map2(nb_keys$stratum, nb_keys$spec_id, function(this_stratum, this_spec) {
    this_fit_id <- model_specs$fit_id[model_specs$spec_id == this_spec]
    sf <- stratum_fits[[paste0(this_stratum, "__", this_fit_id)]]
    kept <- selection_long %>%
      filter(stratum == this_stratum, spec_id == this_spec) %>%
      retained_variables()
    union(sf$forced, setdiff(kept, sf$forced))
  }),
  nb_keys$key
)

nb_fits <- purrr::imap(spec_terms, function(term_vars, this_key) {
  this_stratum <- sub("__.*$", "", this_key)
  fit_nb(strata[[this_stratum]], term_vars, outcome_var)
})

nb_nulls <- purrr::map(
  stats::setNames(strata_levels, strata_levels),
  ~ fit_nb(strata[[.x]], character(0), outcome_var)
)

for (this_key in names(nb_fits)) {
  if (!is.null(nb_fits[[this_key]])) {
    saveRDS(nb_fits[[this_key]], paste0(fits_folder, "nb_", this_key, ".rds"))
  }
}
saveRDS(nb_nulls, paste0(fits_folder, "nb_nulls.rds"))

stratum_deff <- stats::setNames(stratum_inventory$kish_deff, stratum_inventory$stratum)

nb_coefficients <- purrr::imap_dfr(nb_fits, function(fit, this_key) {
  if (is.null(fit)) return(tibble::tibble())
  this_stratum <- sub("__.*$", "", this_key)
  this_spec <- sub("^.*__", "", this_key)
  this_fit_id <- model_specs$fit_id[model_specs$spec_id == this_spec]
  column_map <- stratum_fits[[paste0(this_stratum, "__", this_fit_id)]]$design$map
  tidy_nb(fit, column_map, deff = stratum_deff[[this_stratum]]) %>%
    mutate(stratum = this_stratum, spec_id = this_spec)
}) %>%
  left_join(model_specs %>% select(spec_id, model_label, role), by = "spec_id") %>%
  mutate(
    domain = variable_domains[variable],
    variable_label = variable_labels[variable],
    term = paste0(variable_label, ifelse(level == "", "", paste0(": ", level)))
  )

readr::write_csv(nb_coefficients, paste0(local_data, "nb-coefficients.csv"))
Output out5: Variance-estimation instruments for Section 5.9
Section 5.9 asks for 500 bootstrap replicate weights, the same instrument
Sections 5.3, 5.5 and 5.7 ask for. They do not exist in the 2010 or 2014
PUMF (inherited decision 10), and strata and PSU identifiers are
suppressed, so no fully design-based variance estimator can be built for
either stratum. What follows are two LOWER bounds on how far the
model-based intervals understate uncertainty. Neither sees clustering.

Both instruments are close to their model-1 values, which is what a
stratification of a large sample should produce: halving a sample does not
change how unequal its weights are. Table t62 reports all three interval
variants side by side and marks terms whose standard error exceeds 2
on the log scale (decision 40).

The design effect is computed within each stratum rather than inherited from the pooled sample, because a design effect describes the weight distribution of the sample whose intervals it widens. Both instruments should land close to their model-1 values, and that is the expected result rather than a reassuring one: halving a sample does not change how unequal its weights are.

Table t6 (deliverable Table 5): Adjusted prevalence rate ratios with 95% Wald intervals for every term retained inside each sex stratum, under all four Section 5.4 specifications. An asterisk marks Wald p < 0.05; an exclamation mark flags a term whose standard error exceeds 2 on the log scale (decision 40). A blank cell means the term was not retained by that specification. These are NOT bootstrap intervals (inherited decision 10), and they ignore the selection step that produced the term list. Table t62 carries the log-scale coefficients, standard errors, exact p-values and two wider interval variants; Table t65 carries the female-male comparison, which this table deliberately does not support.

Table t62 is the compliance artifact: every quantity Section 5.9 names — unweighted \(n\), weighted \(N\), coefficient, standard error, prevalence rate ratio, interval and Wald \(p\)-value — for every term in every sex-stratified model. Read the three interval columns together, as in model-1: where the Wald and Kish intervals agree about whether they contain 1, the conclusion survives the weighting problem; where they disagree, the term is unresolved rather than null or significant.

The comparison Section 5.9 actually asks for

Tables t6 and t62 report the two models. They do not — and cannot — report the difference between them, because a term is present in one of them and absent from the other for two reasons that the tables cannot separate: the association may be absent, or the penalty may simply have declined to select it. Reading a blank cell as a null is the single most likely misreading of Table 5, and it is a misreading the table’s own structure invites.

Decision 39 removes the ambiguity by refitting both strata, without penalty, on the union of the terms either stratum retained under the primary specification. Every term then has an estimate on both sides. What the penalty did is reported separately, as a fact about the procedure, in the “Retained in” column.

Table t65: The female-male comparison Section 5.9 asks for. Both strata are refitted without penalty on the union of the terms either retained under the primary specification (decision 39), so every term has an estimate on both sides and ‘not selected’ is never mistaken for ‘null’. ‘Retained in’ records what the penalty did; the estimates record what the data say. The ratio of rate ratios is the multiplicative difference between the female and male associations, and its interval and z-test use se = sqrt(se_F^2 + se_M^2), which is valid because the two strata are disjoint samples. Rows are ordered by p; the table is a screen for heterogeneity, NOT a set of confirmatory tests - it carries 10 comparisons with no multiplicity control, and all of them inherit the selection step that produced the union set.

Table t65 is this report’s central artifact and the reason model-3 is not simply model-1 run twice. Three columns are read together. “Retained in” says what the selection procedure did. “PR female” and “PR male” say what the data say, for every term, on both sides. “Ratio F / M” is the multiplicative gap between them, with an interval built from the two independent stratum standard errors.

The rows worth attention are the ones where those two accounts disagree — a term retained in only one stratum whose ratio of rate ratios is nonetheless close to 1 is a selection artifact, not a sex difference; a term retained in both whose ratio is far from 1 is a sex difference that the selection grid conceals entirely.

Table t65 is a screen, not a set of tests

Every \(p\)-value in it is a single-comparison Wald test, computed over a term set that a LASSO chose using the same respondents. There is no multiplicity control, and the selection step is not accounted for in any of the intervals. The table’s purpose is to rank candidate sex differences so that a small number can be discussed with the care they need — not to certify any of them. The Kish-inflated \(p\)-value column is there as a reminder of how much of the apparent precision belongs to the assumption of simple random sampling.

Graph g5 is Table t65 in the form that makes the comparison visible: each term appears twice, once per stratum, ordered by the size of the gap. The top and bottom of each domain panel are where Section 5.9 has something to say; the middle is where the two sexes agree.

Graph g51 plots the difference itself rather than the two estimates. A point at 1 means the association is identical in the two strata; distance from 1 is the size of the sex difference and the interval is its uncertainty. The filled points are a screening device with the same caveat as Table t65 attached: with this many comparisons and no multiplicity control, some intervals will exclude 1 by construction.

Table t61: Section 5.10 metrics computed IN SAMPLE, for all eight sex-stratified models. RMSE and MAE are weighted (inherited decision 19). AIC and BIC come from a weighted pseudo-likelihood and rank models rather than measure them (inherited decision 18); ACROSS strata they are not comparable at all, because each is computed on a different sample. Read them down a stratum, never across. The held-out versions, which are the ones Section 5.10 actually asks for, are in Tables t63 and t64.

One warning about Table t61 that it shares with model-2’s version: the rows are not comparable across strata. Each is computed on a different sample with a different outcome distribution, and AIC and BIC come from a weighted pseudo-likelihood on different data. Read the table down a stratum — comparing the four specifications within one sex — and never across. The dispersion parameter is the one exception, and only because decision 37 rescales the weights inside each stratum specifically to make it comparable.

Output out3 answers Section 5.9’s request that non-convergence be reported, and counts empty selections. The empty-selection count is also the direct evidence for decision 35: if the parsimonious penalty returns something in every stratum, Section 5.5’s designation of it as primary needs no amendment, and model-2’s reversal stays confined to the subgroups that motivated it.

Review point 8

Agree or disagree that Tables t6, t62 and t65 together are fit to serve as the study’s Table 5. Four questions:

  1. Should the deliverable table carry all four specifications, or should Model 1 stand alone with the rest in an appendix?
  2. Is decision 39’s union model the right basis for the female–male comparison? The alternatives — comparing the two selected models directly, or restricting to terms selected in both — are recorded with it. Both are simpler and both are more likely to be misread.
  3. Should Table t65 carry any multiplicity adjustment, or is a screen presented as a screen the honest presentation? Adjusting would change what the table is for.
  4. Is the UNSTABLE flag at a standard error of 2 on the log scale the right threshold at this sample size? It was set for model-2’s small subgroups and re-made here; at stratum scale it may be too permissive to catch anything.

Step 9 — Section 5.10, Held-Out Performance

Section 5.10 asks for AIC, BIC, McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\), a C-statistic, and RMSE and MAE “computed on the withheld test fold,” averaged over five folds, for each sex-stratified model. Table t61 gave the in-sample versions. This step supplies the rest.

Unlike Section 5.8, Section 5.10 does not offer leave-one-out as an alternative — which is consistent, because both strata are large. Five folds also keep model-3 on the same footing as model-1 and model-2. Decision 38.

Five-fold cross-validation of every stratum and specification, both variants 
if (!force_refit_cv && file.exists(cv_cache_path)) {
  cv_performance <- readRDS(cv_cache_path)
  cat("Loaded cached cross-validation results from ", cv_cache_path, "\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("Refitting the Section 5.10 cross-validation. This is the slow block.\n")
  cv_start_time <- Sys.time()

  cv_performance <- purrr::map_dfr(strata_levels, function(this_stratum) {
    sub <- strata[[this_stratum]]
    fold_id <- assign_folds(nrow(sub), perf_folds, perf_seed)
    cat("  ", this_stratum, " (n = ", nrow(sub), ")\n", sep = "")

    purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(perf_folds), function(this_fold) {
      cat("    fold ", this_fold, " of ", perf_folds, "\n", sep = "")
      test_rows <- which(fold_id == this_fold)
      train_rows <- which(fold_id != this_fold)

      # Variant A - term set fixed at what the whole stratum selected.
      fixed <- purrr::map_dfr(model_specs$spec_id, function(this_spec) {
        term_vars <- spec_terms[[paste0(this_stratum, "__", this_spec)]]
        evaluate_fold(sub, train_rows, test_rows, term_vars, outcome_var) %>%
          mutate(stratum = this_stratum, spec_id = this_spec,
                 fold = this_fold, variant = "fixed term set")
      })

      # Variant B - the whole two-stage procedure re-run inside the training
      # fold, so no held-out respondent contributed to selection. One penalised
      # fit per predictor set, shared by the two penalties that read it.
      train_frame <- droplevels(sub[train_rows, , drop = FALSE])
      fold_forced <- forced_vars[
        purrr::map_lgl(forced_vars, ~ is_informative(train_frame[[.x]]))
      ]
      fold_lassos <- purrr::map(
        stats::setNames(fit_ids, fit_ids),
        function(this_fit_id) {
          offered <- stratum_candidates(train_frame, candidate_sets[[this_fit_id]])
          design <- build_design(train_frame, c(fold_forced, offered))
          list(
            design = design,
            lasso = tryCatch(
              fit_lasso(design, train_frame[[outcome_var]],
                        train_frame$weight_scaled, lasso_seed),
              error = function(e) NULL
            )
          )
        }
      )

      reselected <- purrr::pmap_dfr(
        model_specs %>% select(spec_id, lambda_rule, fit_id),
        function(spec_id, lambda_rule, fit_id) {
          fl <- fold_lassos[[fit_id]]
          term_vars <- if (is.null(fl$lasso)) {
            fold_forced
          } else {
            kept <- coefficients_at(fl$lasso, fl$design, lambda_rule) %>%
              retained_variables()
            union(fold_forced, setdiff(kept, fold_forced))
          }
          evaluate_fold(sub, train_rows, test_rows, term_vars, outcome_var) %>%
            mutate(stratum = this_stratum, spec_id = spec_id,
                   fold = this_fold, variant = "selection re-run",
                   n_vars_selected = length(term_vars))
        }
      )

      bind_rows(fixed, reselected)
    })
  }) %>%
    left_join(model_specs %>% select(spec_id, model_label, role), by = "spec_id")

  attr(cv_performance, "elapsed_minutes") <-
    as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), cv_start_time, units = "mins"))
  saveRDS(cv_performance, cv_cache_path)
}

readr::write_csv(cv_performance, paste0(local_data, "cv-performance-folds.csv"))

cv_summary <- cv_performance %>%
  group_by(variant, stratum, spec_id, model_label) %>%
  summarise(
    folds_converged = sum(converged),
    n_terms_mean = mean(n_terms, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_terms_range = if (all(is.na(n_terms))) {
      "n/a"
    } else {
      paste0(min(n_terms, na.rm = TRUE), "-", max(n_terms, na.rm = TRUE))
    },
    rmse_mean = mean(rmse, na.rm = TRUE), rmse_sd = stats::sd(rmse, na.rm = TRUE),
    mae_mean = mean(mae, na.rm = TRUE), mae_sd = stats::sd(mae, na.rm = TRUE),
    mcfadden_mean = mean(mcfadden_r2, na.rm = TRUE),
    mcfadden_sd = stats::sd(mcfadden_r2, na.rm = TRUE),
    c_mean = mean(c_statistic, na.rm = TRUE), c_sd = stats::sd(c_statistic, na.rm = TRUE),
    comparable_share = mean(comparable_share, na.rm = TRUE),
    unscorable = sum(n_unscorable, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(stratum_inventory %>% select(stratum, n), by = "stratum") %>%
  arrange(variant, match(stratum, strata_levels), spec_id)

readr::write_csv(cv_summary, paste0(local_data, "cv-performance-summary.csv"))

Table t64 removes that advantage by re-running the whole two-stage procedure inside each training fold. The term-count range is the column to read first. Model 1 found the selected set unstable even at \(n = 48{,}932\), ranging from eight to thirty-eight terms across folds; a stratum is about half that, so a wider range here is the expected result and a narrow one would be the surprise.

Graph g6 shows the five folds individually rather than only their mean, for the primary specification. The comparison it is built for is between the spread of the folds and the gap between the two strata. Where the fold points scatter more widely than the strata differ, a difference in held-out performance between the sexes is not a difference, and the means printed in Tables t63 and t64 should not be set side by side without that qualification.

Harrell's C counts a pair only when the two respondents differ on the
outcome. Most respondents in both strata report zero days, so most pairs
are incomparable and never enter the denominator. Table t63 reports the
comparable share beside every C for exactly this reason, and the female
and male C-statistics should be compared only alongside those shares.

A positive d McFadden or d C is the amount by which evaluating a model on

The C-statistic needs its comparable-pairs share

Harrell’s C counts only pairs of respondents who differ on the outcome. Most respondents in both strata report zero days, so most pairs are incomparable and never enter the denominator — and the share that does enter is not the same in the two strata, because the strata do not have the same proportion of respondents with a non-zero outcome. A female and a male C-statistic are therefore computed over different fractions of their respective samples, and comparing them without the comparable-pairs share beside each is not a valid comparison. Table t63 reports the share on every row for exactly this reason.

Review point 9

Three questions.

  1. Which table is the Section 5.10 deliverable — t63, which follows the proposal’s wording, or t64, which is what the numbers would be on new data? Model 1 found the gap negligible; whether that holds at stratum scale is what out6 measures, and the answer should decide this.
  2. Does the term-count range in t64 change how a sex-specific variable list may be described in the manuscript? If the selected set moves substantially under refitting, the honest sentence is about the estimates in Table t65 rather than about the identity of either stratum’s selected set.
  3. Should the female and male models be compared on held-out performance at all? Section 5.10 asks for the metrics per model and does not ask for the comparison; Graph g6 supplies it because the question is natural, but the comparable-pairs problem means it is easy to over-read.

What Model 3 Settles, and What It Does Not

Settled.

  • The stratifying variable is established as DHH_SEX and the report is committed to saying sex rather than gender, with the reason recorded rather than assumed.
  • The two strata are shown to partition the Section 5.5 analytic sample exactly, so Table 5 describes the same respondents as Table 3, with no overlap and no loss.
  • The composition difference between the strata is measured before any model is fitted, so that a later asymmetry in selection can be checked against prevalence rather than attributed to association by default.
  • Section 5.9. A sex-stratified model is estimated for each sex under all four Section 5.4 specifications, with both sample sizes reported.
  • Deliverable Table 5 is produced in two forms: a rate-ratio grid (t6) and a full ledger carrying log coefficients, standard errors, exact \(p\)-values and three interval variants (t62).
  • The female–male comparison Section 5.9 asks for is delivered on a basis that cannot confuse “not selected” with “null” (t65, g5, g51), and the selection asymmetry is reported separately as a fact about the procedure.
  • Section 5.10. All five requested metrics are reported, in-sample (t61) and on withheld folds (t63), with an honest-selection counterpart (t64) that quantifies how much of the apparent performance is optimism and how far each stratum’s selected set moves under refitting.
  • Non-convergence and empty selections are counted and named.
  • Ten new decisions are named, resolved, and marked for reversal.

Not settled.

  • Variance estimation. Inherited decision 10 is data-blocked. The sandwich and Kish intervals bracket the understatement from below; neither is the quantity Section 5.9 specifies. Delivering it requires Research Data Centre access.
  • Gender. Neither cycle carries a gender item, so a gender-stratified analysis is not available from these files at any level of effort.
  • The sex differences themselves. Table t65 ranks candidates; it does not certify any of them. Every row carries the selection step in its interval and none carries a multiplicity adjustment. Confirming a specific sex difference is a pre-registered, single-hypothesis exercise that these data can motivate but not complete.
  • Composition versus association. Where a sex difference coincides with a prevalence difference in Table t21, the two explanations are not separated here. Separating them requires a reweighting or decomposition analysis that answers a different question from the one Section 5.9 asks.
  • Section 5.1. Little’s MCAR test and multiple imputation are not performed; complete-case analysis stands in, inherited from model-1 along with its cost.
  • Model adequacy inside strata. Whether a negative binomial is the right likelihood for a stratum outcome that is still majority zeros is not tested here, any more than it was in model-1 or model-2. Calibration, rootograms and hurdle alternatives belong to a dedicated evaluation report reading the artifacts in Step 10.

How to use this report. Model 3 is the estimation of record for Sections 5.9 and 5.10. With it, every modelling section of the proposal has an estimation of record: 5.3 in model-00, 5.4 to 5.6 in model-1, 5.7 to 5.8 in model-2, and 5.9 to 5.10 here. Reports that follow should load the objects in Table t7 and interpret them; re-estimating would produce a second set of numbers with no better claim to authority and a real chance of drifting from these.
